The Po Engine is currently used by CERT-ISAC for malware analysis and certification of mobile apps for security and privacy.
Attacks & Cyber threats against India The recent ‘Operation Hangover’ report from Norman’s Malware Detection Team has projected India as an emerging APT actor.
While the statistics presented by CERT-In looks alarming by itself, the actual state of domains that end with “gov.in”, is much worse.
A quick look at the following recent screenshot of www.zone-h.org site provides some shocking insight.
These documents exploited previously known vulnerabilities ( CVE-2012-0158 and CVE-2010-3333 ) to drop “Travnet” malware onto the systems.
 “Army Cyber Security Policy 2013.doc”  “Jallianwala bagh massacre a deeply shameful act.doc”  “Report - Asia Defense Spending Boom.doc”
We managed to acquired 2 variants of the “Travnet” malware & our analysis of the same is as follows.
Filename travnet_A.exe Filesize 97792 bytes Filetype PE32 executable (GUI) Intel 80386, for MS Windows A quick analysis by PEiD reveals that the binary is not packed or protected.
Next step is to create a configuration file named “config_t.dat” in the windows' “system” folder.
Batch file : temp.bat Configuration file : config_t.dat
Next section focuses on the analysis of the DLL (“6to4ex.dll”) that was dropped by this executable.
Analysis of “6to4ex.dll” File Details Filename 6to4ex.dll Filetype PE32 executable (DLL) (GUI) Intel 80386, for MS Windows
Filename : “system_t.dll” Upon proper character encoding & use of google's Translate feature, it turns out to be “Chinese”.
It also uploads the list of files found on the victim machine, which was saved in the “enumfs.ini” file to the remote server, by copying its contents to a new file, named following this format:
Filename travnet_B.exe Filetype PE32 executable (GUI) Intel 80386, for MS Windows Filesize 102400 bytes A quick analysis by PEiD reveals that the binary is not packed or protected.
It achieves persistence by copying itself to the currently logged-in user's “temp” folder as “csmss.exe” & placing a shortcut to it, named as “seruvice.lnk” in the “startup” folder.
Then it checks if the victim machine is connected to the internet or not, by trying to resolve “smtp.live.com” & if that fails, as a second attempt, “smtp..yahoo.com”.

Apart from that, this variant also creates a file that lists all the currently running processes on the victim machine, into a text file named “Process.dll” inside the currently logged-on user's “temp” folder.
Travnet Technical Analysis : Part C Apart from analyzing the malware samples, we also tried to gather as much information about the C&C servers as we could.
The fact that even after a lot of research papers being published on the analysis of the Travnet malware, some of the C&C servers are still active & functioning, is noteworthy.
 www.pkspring.net  www.viprambler.com
Let’s start with the analysis of “ www.viprambler.com ”.
The Travnet C&C hosted at “pkspring.net” seems to be fully functional & active all the time.
“Pkspring.net” WHOIS data (Recent)
A search for the email “ livep92@hotmail.com ” led us to the following page :
We did some research on the current status of one of the domains from the above list, “discoverypeace.org”.
The current WHOIS data for the domain “discoverypeace.org” is as follows:
This looks strikingly similar to the current status of the active C&C domain “pkstring.net”.
It’s also a known fact the Indian government & other important sectors from India were heavily targeted during this campaign.
Use of Outdated Software on Government Websites Another interesting finding is the fact that many of the servers that host “gov.in” sites are running outdated software versions.
As an example, from the above image, it is evident that the domain “karnataka.gov.in” is hosted on a server running “Windows Server 2003”, on 22-June-2013.
The next part of this research paper focuses on a recent APT campaign against multiple countries including India was targeted.

While each and every technical cause for weak Indian Cyber space is beyond the scope of this document, we also believe that India requires a strong policy driven approach along with inspiring leadership from thought leaders and Government departments in Information security to bring the much needed change.

To summarize the modus operandi of the attack, targeted phishing mails were sent to individuals, having Office documents as attachments. These documents exploited previously known vulnerabilities ( CVE-2012-0158 and CVE-2010-3333 ) to drop “Travnet” malware onto the systems. Its fascinating to note that the attachments that were sent to Indian targets were carefully selected & some of them were named as follows:
Filename travnet_A.exe
MD5 d286c4cdf40e2dae5362eff562bccd3a
SHA256 a75fdd9e52643dc7a1790c79cbfffe9348f80a9b0984eafd90723bf7ca68f4ce
Next step is to create a configuration file named “config_t.dat” in the windows' “system” folder.
Configuration file : config_t.dat
Next section focuses on the analysis of the DLL (“6to4ex.dll”) that was dropped by this executable.
Filename 6to4ex.dll
MD5 452660884ebe3e88ddabe2b340113c8a
SHA1 b80d436afcf2f0493f2317ff1a38c9ba329f24b1

“enumfs.ini” as the name suggests, is a complete list of all files and folders on the computer. “dnlist.ini” seems to be noting down the date & time. “system_t.dll” on the other hand, contains a broad category of sensitive information about the computer like the “Computer Name”, Windows version, IP address, list of running processes, network information & so on. The contents of the files are as follows
Filename : “system_t.dll”

To summarize, the Travnet malware initially collects system information, a list of files on the victim machine among others, then sends this data to the remote Command & Control (C&C) server, by using custom compression & encoding functions. The malware creates a new file with the naming convention as follows : “travlerbackinfo-%d-%d-%d-%d-%d.dll”, where the signed integer values are replaced by the current system date & time, copies the content of “system_t.dll” into it & then, uploads it to the C&C.
Filename travnet_B.exe
SHA1 dc63b4b9ee2f8486b96ce62be4a31e041d422ef7
SHA256 e547e8a8bc27d65dca92bc861be82e1c94b9c9aca8a2b75381e9b16e4ad89600
It achieves persistence by copying itself to the currently logged-in user's “temp” folder as “csmss.exe” & placing a shortcut to it, named as “seruvice.lnk” in the “startup” folder.

Apart from that, this variant also creates a file that lists all the currently running processes on the victim machine, into a text file named “Process.dll” inside the currently logged-on user's “temp” folder. This variant also uses a modified naming convention to upload files onto the remote C&C.
